topics.title: Year 3 wonderful words 1
topics.intro: Year 3 readers meet harder words. Many of these come from the stories you will read: placid, sternly, scornful…
topics.teach: Use “reckless” and “cautious” in two sentences about racing drivers.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to use one of today’s words to describe someone in the family (kindly!).

topics.title: Year 3 wonderful words 2
topics.intro: More powerful words for reading and writing: resourceful, intrepid, ominous…
topics.talk: Play “mime the word”: {she} acts out stealthy, nimble or frantic, and you guess.

topics.title: Similes, metaphors and sound words
topics.intro: Writers paint pictures with words. A simile says something is LIKE something else. A metaphor says it IS something else. Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like its meaning: crash, poop-poop!
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor, with an example of each.
topics.talk: In the car, take turns making similes: “as fast as…”, “as loud as…”.

topics.title: Kinds of writing
topics.intro: Instructions, letters, recounts, reports and persuasive writing all have their own features. Spotting them helps you read faster and write better.
topics.teach: Explain three features of a set of instructions.
topics.talk: Find a recipe together and ask {him} to point out the features of instructions.

head: kind of writing
look out for
rows: a title, a list of equipment, numbered steps starting with verbs like “Mix” or “Cut”
starts with “Dear…”, ends with “Yours sincerely” or “Love from”
the past tense and time words: First, Next, After that, Finally
organised by topic, with headings, facts and a glossary
strong opinions and exciting words to make you do or believe something

topics.title: Just So Stories: the Whale
topics.intro: Rudyard Kipling wrote these funny “how it happened” stories more than 120 years ago for his own children. He talks straight to the reader, calling you “O my Best Beloved”. Read them aloud!
topics.teach: Explain why Kipling keeps reminding the reader about the suspenders.
topics.talk: Read “How the Whale Got His Throat” aloud together, with lots of expression.

topics.title: The Wind in the Willows: Toad and the motor-car
topics.intro: Mr Toad, Ratty and Mole are on a trip in a canary-coloured horse and cart, when a motor-car roars past. Kenneth Grahame wrote this in 1908, when cars were brand new and amazing. The sentences are long, so read slowly.
topics.teach: Explain how Toad’s feelings about the motor-car are different from Rat’s.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} thinks Toad will do next. (In the book, he buys a car!)

topics.title: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
topics.intro: Lewis Carroll’s famous story was published in 1865. Alice is bored on a riverbank when something very strange runs past.
topics.teach: Explain what made Alice suddenly curious about the White Rabbit.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would do if a rabbit with a pocket watch ran past.

topics.title: The Jungle Book: a man’s cub
topics.intro: Rudyard Kipling also wrote The Jungle Book, about a boy called Mowgli who is raised by wolves in India. Here is the night the wolves find him.
topics.teach: Explain why Mother Wolf is surprised by the baby.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how {she} thinks the wolves will look after a human baby.

topics.title: Myths and legends
topics.intro: Myths are ancient stories about gods, heroes and monsters. Legends are old stories that may have a little truth in them. Heroes have been around a lot longer than comics!
topics.teach: Explain what a myth is, using Theseus or Icarus as an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which hero is the bravest: Theseus, Arthur or George?

topics.title: New adventures: rain, meteors and a flood
topics.intro: Three new adventures. As you read, think about what the characters learn, and how the writer makes you feel tense.
topics.teach: Explain what Turbo, Captain Nova and the superhero each learned.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which story was the most exciting and which words made it exciting.

topics.title: Fact files: Romans, planets and bees
topics.intro: Three fact files. Use the headings, numbers and glossary to find information quickly.
topics.teach: Explain how a glossary helps a reader.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for one fact from each fact file.

topics.title: Poems: pirates, lamplighters and a bed-boat
topics.intro: Four more poems by Robert Louis Stevenson, about a child’s imagination: a pirate ship in a meadow, toy soldiers in the bed, and a bed that sails away at night.
topics.teach: Explain how the child in “Pirate Story” turns a garden into the sea.
topics.talk: Read “The Lamplighter” together and talk about how streets were lit before electricity.

topics.title: Classics: the Sand-fairy and Black Beauty
topics.intro: Two more classics, with longer sentences and old-fashioned words: a grumpy magical creature dug up in a gravel pit, and a horse telling his own story.
topics.teach: Explain how the writer shows that the Sand-fairy is grumpy.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} would like to find a Sand-fairy, and what {she} would wish for.

topics.title: Year 4 wonderful words
topics.intro: Words that Year 4 and 5 readers use: perilous, exhilarating, meticulous…
topics.talk: Ask {him} to describe a racing car using “exhilarating”.

items.prompt: What does “reckless” mean?
items.explain: reckless: not caring about danger. “The reckless driver took the bend far too fast.”
items.learn:
**reckless** means not caring about danger.
_The reckless driver took the bend far too fast._

items.prompt: What does “scornful” mean?
items.explain: scornful: sneering and mocking. “The creature gave Jane’s hat a scornful look.”
items.learn:
**scornful** means sneering and mocking.
_The creature gave Jane’s hat a scornful look._

items.prompt: What does “placid” mean?
items.explain: placid: calm and peaceful. “After the crash, Toad wore a placid, happy expression.”
items.learn:
**placid** means calm and peaceful.
_After the crash, Toad wore a placid, happy expression._

items.prompt: What does “sternly” mean?
items.explain: sternly: in a strict, serious way. ““Are you coming to help us?” Rat demanded sternly.”
items.learn:

items.prompt: What does “bewildered” mean?

items.learn:

items.prompt: What does “courageous” mean?
items.explain: courageous: very brave. “The courageous knight faced the dragon.”
items.learn:
**courageous** means very brave.
_The courageous knight faced the dragon._

items.explain: cautious: careful to avoid danger. “Captain Nova was cautious near the meteors.”
items.learn:
**cautious** means careful to avoid danger.
_Captain Nova was cautious near the meteors._

items.learn:

items.prompt: What does “frantic” mean?

items.learn:
**frantic** means wild with worry or hurry.
_Bleep beeped in a frantic voice._

items.prompt: What does “majestic” mean?

items.learn:

items.learn:
**inquisitive** means eager to find things out.

items.explain: tranquil: calm and quiet. “The tranquil lake shone in the moonlight.”
items.learn:
**tranquil** means calm and quiet.
_The tranquil lake shone in the moonlight._

items.prompt: What does “desolate” mean?
items.explain: desolate: empty, bleak and lonely. “The rover crossed a desolate red desert.”
items.learn:
**desolate** means empty, bleak and lonely.

items.prompt: What does “formidable” mean?

items.learn:

items.learn:
**ravenous** means extremely hungry.

items.learn:

items.prompt: What does “valiant” mean?
items.explain: valiant: very brave and determined. “Theseus made a valiant journey into the maze.”
items.learn:
**valiant** means very brave and determined.
_Theseus made a valiant journey into the maze._

items.prompt: What does “immense” mean?
items.explain: immense: very, very large. “The immense motor-car filled the whole road.”
items.learn:
**immense** means very, very large.

items.prompt: What does “sagacious” mean?
items.explain: sagacious: wise and sensible. “The sagacious owl gave good advice.”
items.learn:
**sagacious** means wise and sensible.
_The sagacious owl gave good advice._

items.prompt: Which of these is a simile?

options.text: The car was as fast as lightning.
The car was lightning on the track.
options.feedback: That says the car IS lightning: a metaphor.
There is no comparison here.

items.explain: A simile compares using “like” or “as”: as fast as lightning.

items.prompt: Which of these is a metaphor?

options.text: The classroom was like a zoo.
options.feedback: “like” makes it a simile.
That just describes it; it doesn’t compare.

items.explain: A metaphor says one thing IS another: the classroom was a zoo (very noisy and wild!).

items.prompt: Which sentence gives a non-human thing human feelings or actions (personification)?

options.text: The wind whispered through the trees.
The wind was strong and very cold today.
options.feedback: That is a plain description.

options.text: The wind was as fierce as a lion.
options.feedback: That is a simile.

items.explain: Wind cannot really whisper: the writer is treating it like a person.

items.prompt: Which word is onomatopoeia (it sounds like the noise it describes)?

options.feedback: “quiet” doesn’t make a sound when you say it.
Say “sizzle” aloud: it sounds like frying!

items.explain: Onomatopoeia: bang, crash, sizzle, buzz… and Toad’s “Poop-poop!”

items.prompt: Which phrase uses alliteration (words starting with the same sound)?

options.feedback: b, r, b: not all the same sound.
o, g, h: different sounds.

items.explain: Alliteration repeats the first sound: ten tiny tigers. Writers use it to make phrases memorable.

items.prompt: A simile usually uses which two words to compare?
items.explain: as brave as a lion; ran like the wind.

items.prompt: In The Wind in the Willows, a car’s hum is “like the drone of a distant bee”. What does this simile tell you?

options.text: The car was full of angry bees
options.feedback: It only SOUNDED like a bee.

options.text: The car was very small and yellow
options.feedback: The simile is about the sound, not the size or colour.

items.explain: Comparing the far-off car to a bee helps you hear its quiet hum.

items.prompt: Why do writers use similes and metaphors?

options.text: To help the reader picture things

options.feedback: They often make sentences longer, but richer.

options.text: Because the rules of writing say so
options.feedback: It is a choice, to paint a picture in the reader’s mind.

items.explain: Comparisons make pictures in the reader’s head.

items.prompt: “The moon was a silver coin in the sky.” What is this?

options.feedback: There is no “like” or “as”: it says the moon WAS a coin.
No sound words here.

items.explain: It says the moon IS a coin: a metaphor.

items.prompt: “The knight was brave, strong and loyal.” Writers often use a group of three like this. Why?

options.text: Two describing words are not allowed
options.feedback: Writers can use any number; three just sounds good.
These words don’t rhyme.

items.explain: Groups of three have a satisfying rhythm: “Ready, steady, go!”

items.prompt: “The crab and the dab, and the plaice and the dace, and the skate and his mate”. What makes this fun to read aloud?

options.text: It is very quiet and calm
options.feedback: Say it aloud: crab/dab, plaice/dace, skate/mate rhyme!

options.text: It has no rhythm at all
options.feedback: It bounces along with rhymes and rhythm.

items.explain: Kipling loved the sound of words. The rhyming pairs make the list bounce along.

items.prompt: “I’ve told you a million times!” is an example of…

options.feedback: There is no “like” or “as”.
Nobody has really said it a million times!

items.explain: Exaggeration (hyperbole) makes a point stronger. It isn’t meant to be taken literally.

items.prompt: Which is a feature of instructions?

options.feedback: That is a letter.
That is a poem.

items.explain: Instructions: a title saying what you will make or do, a list of equipment, and numbered steps starting with verbs like “Mix” or “Cut”.

items.prompt: How might a formal letter end?

options.feedback: That ends a story.
That ends a set of instructions.

items.explain: Letters start with “Dear…” and end with “Yours sincerely” or “Love from”.

items.prompt: A recount tells about something that has already happened. Which tense does it mostly use?

options.feedback: Recounts tell what happened, not what will happen.
Commands are for instructions.

items.explain: Recounts (like a diary or a news report) use the past tense and time words: First, Next, After that, Finally.

items.prompt: Which sentence is trying to PERSUADE you?

options.text: You simply must visit the amazing Speedway Museum!
The Speedway Museum opens at 9 o’clock.
options.feedback: That gives a fact; it is not trying to change your mind.

options.text: I went to the Speedway Museum.
options.feedback: That is a recount.

items.explain: Persuasive writing uses strong opinions and exciting words to make you do or believe something.

items.prompt: What is a glossary?

options.text: A list of tricky words and meanings
A list of chapters at the front
options.feedback: That is the contents page.

options.text: All the pictures in a book
options.feedback: Those are illustrations.

items.explain: A glossary explains the special words used in a non-fiction book.

items.prompt: Where would you look to find which page the chapter on volcanoes starts on?

options.feedback: The glossary explains words.
The cover shows the title and author.

items.explain: The contents page, at the front, lists chapters and their page numbers.

items.prompt: An index is at the back of a book. How is it organised?

options.text: In the order the pages come
options.feedback: That is the contents. An index is alphabetical.

options.text: By the colour of each page
options.feedback: It is alphabetical.

items.explain: Look up “Saturn” under S in the index to find every page about it.

items.prompt: A fact file about bees with headings like “The hive” and “Making honey” is called a…

options.feedback: It gives facts, not a made-up plot.
It isn’t telling you how to do something.

items.explain: Non-chronological means “not in time order”: it is organised by topic, with headings.

items.prompt: Why do fact files have headings and subheadings?

options.text: To help you find facts quickly

options.feedback: They help you find things.

options.text: Because all stories need them at the top
options.feedback: Stories don’t usually have headings.

items.explain: Headings tell you what each section is about, so you can skip to the part you need.

items.prompt: What is the difference between fiction and non-fiction?

options.text: Fiction is made up; non-fiction gives true information
Fiction is always long; non-fiction is short
options.feedback: Either can be long or short.
Both can have pictures.

items.explain: The Rain Race is fiction. The planets fact file is non-fiction.

items.prompt: Why was there only one small fish left in all the sea?

options.text: The others had swum far away
options.feedback: “All the fishes he could find in all the sea he ate with his mouth.”
It was the Whale!

items.explain: The Whale ate every fish he could find.
items.passage:
In the sea, once upon a time, O my Best Beloved, there was a Whale, and he ate fishes. He ate the starfish and the garfish, and the crab and the dab, and the plaice and the dace, and the skate and his mate, and the mackereel and the pickereel, and the really truly twirly-whirly eel. All the fishes he could find in all the sea he ate with his mouth—so! Till at last there was only one small fish left in all the sea, and he was a small ’Stute Fish, and he swam a little behind the Whale’s right ear, so as to be out of harm’s way. Then the Whale stood up on his tail and said, ‘I’m hungry.’ And the small ’Stute Fish said in a small ’stute voice, ‘Noble and generous Cetacean, have you ever tasted Man?’

‘No,’ said the Whale. ‘What is it like?’

‘Nice,’ said the small ’Stute Fish. ‘Nice but nubbly.’

‘Then fetch me some,’ said the Whale, and he made the sea froth up with his tail.

‘One at a time is enough,’ said the ’Stute Fish. ‘If you swim to latitude Fifty North, longitude Forty West (that is magic), you will find, sitting on a raft, in the middle of the sea, with nothing on but a pair of blue canvas breeches, a pair of suspenders (you must not forget the suspenders, Best Beloved), and a jack-knife, one ship-wrecked Mariner, who, it is only fair to tell you, is a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity.’
items.passageSource: Rudyard Kipling, “How the Whale Got His Throat”, Just So Stories (1902)

items.prompt: Where did the small ’Stute Fish swim, and why?

options.text: Behind the Whale’s right ear, to be out of harm’s way
In front of the Whale’s mouth, to tease him
options.feedback: That would be very dangerous!

options.text: Far away, to find a new sea
options.feedback: He stayed close: “a little behind the Whale’s right ear”.

items.explain: Hiding behind the ear meant the Whale couldn’t easily eat him. That is clever (’stute is short for astute, meaning clever).

items.passage: They were strolling along the high-road easily, the Mole by the horse’s head, talking to him, since the horse had complained that he was being frightfully left out of it, and nobody considered him in the least; the Toad and the Water Rat walking behind the cart talking together—at least Toad was talking, and Rat was saying at intervals, ‘Yes, precisely; and what did YOU say to HIM?’—and thinking all the time of something very different, when far behind them they heard a faint warning hum; like the drone of a distant bee. Glancing back, they saw a small cloud of dust, with a dark centre of energy, advancing on them at incredible speed, while from out the dust a faint ‘Poop-poop!’ wailed like an uneasy animal in pain. items.passage: They were strolling along the high-road easily, the Mole by the horse’s head, talking to him, since the horse had complained that he was being frightfully left out of it, and nobody considered him in the least; the Toad and the Water Rat walking behind the cart talking together—at least Toad was talking, and Rat was saying at intervals, ‘Yes, precisely; and what did YOU say to HIM?’—and thinking all the time of something very different, when far behind them they heard a faint warning hum; like the drone of a distant bee. Glancing back, they saw a small cloud of dust, with a dark centre of energy, advancing on them at incredible speed, while from out the dust a faint ‘Poop-poop!’ wailed like an uneasy animal in pain. Hardly regarding it, they turned to resume their conversation, when in an instant (as it seemed) the peaceful scene was changed, and with a blast of wind and a whirl of sound that made them jump for the nearest ditch, It was on them! The ‘Poop-poop’ rang with a brazen shout in their ears, they had a moment’s glimpse of an interior of glittering plate-glass and rich morocco, and the magnificent motor-car, immense, breath-snatching, passionate, with its pilot tense and hugging his wheel, possessed all earth and air for the fraction of a second, flung an enveloping cloud of dust that blinded and enwrapped them utterly, and then dwindled to a speck in the far distance, changed back into a droning bee once more.

items.passage:
Toad sat straight down in the middle of the dusty road, his legs stretched out before him, and stared fixedly in the direction of the disappearing motor-car. He breathed short, his face wore a placid satisfied expression, and at intervals he faintly murmured ‘Poop-poop!’

The Mole was busy trying to quiet the horse, which he succeeded in doing after a time. Then he went to look at the cart, on its side in the ditch. It was indeed a sorry sight. Panels and windows smashed, axles hopelessly bent, one wheel off, sardine-tins scattered over the wide world, and the bird in the bird-cage sobbing pitifully and calling to be let out.

The Rat came to help him, but their united efforts were not sufficient to right the cart. ‘Hi! Toad!’ they cried. ‘Come and bear a hand, can’t you!’

The Toad never answered a word, or budged from his seat in the road; so they went to see what was the matter with him. They found him in a sort of a trance, a happy smile on his face, his eyes still fixed on the dusty wake of their destroyer. At intervals he was still heard to murmur ‘Poop-poop!’

The Rat shook him by the shoulder. ‘Are you coming to help us, Toad?’ he demanded sternly.

‘Glorious, stirring sight!’ murmured Toad, never offering to move. ‘The poetry of motion! The REAL way to travel! The ONLY way to travel! Here to-day—in next week to-morrow! Villages skipped, towns and cities jumped—always somebody else’s horizon! O bliss! O poop-poop! O my! O my!’

items.passage:
Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, ‘and what is the use of a book,’ thought Alice ‘without pictures or conversations?’

So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.

There was nothing so VERY remarkable in that; nor did Alice think it so VERY much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself, ‘Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!’ (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually TOOK A WATCH OUT OF ITS WAISTCOAT-POCKET, and looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.

In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.

The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.

items.passage:
Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, ‘and what is the use of a book,’ thought Alice ‘without pictures or conversations?’

So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.

There was nothing so VERY remarkable in that; nor did Alice think it so VERY much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself, ‘Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!’ (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually TOOK A WATCH OUT OF ITS WAISTCOAT-POCKET, and looked at it, and then hurried on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.

In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how in the world she was to get out again.

The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.
items.passageSource: Lewis Carroll, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), chapter 1

items.passage:
“Something is coming uphill,” said Mother Wolf, twitching one ear. “Get ready.”

The bushes rustled a little in the thicket, and Father Wolf dropped with his haunches under him, ready for his leap. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world—the wolf checked in mid-spring. He made his bound before he saw what it was he was jumping at, and then he tried to stop himself. The result was that he shot up straight into the air for four or five feet, landing almost where he left ground.

“Man!” he snapped. “A man’s cub. Look!”

Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a naked brown baby who could just walk—as soft and as dimpled a little atom as ever came to a wolf’s cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf’s face, and laughed.

“Is that a man’s cub?” said Mother Wolf. “I have never seen one. Bring it here.”

A Wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg without breaking it, and though Father Wolf’s jaws closed right on the child’s back not a tooth even scratched the skin as he laid it down among the cubs.

“How little! How naked, and—how bold!” said Mother Wolf softly. The baby was pushing his way between the cubs to get close to the warm hide. “Ahai! He is taking his meal with the others. And so this is a man’s cub. Now, was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub among her children?”
items.passageSource: Rudyard Kipling, “Mowgli’s Brothers”, The Jungle Book (1894)

items.passage:
Theseus and the Minotaur

Long ago, on the island of Crete, there lived a cruel king called Minos. Deep beneath his palace was a maze called the Labyrinth, so twisting that nobody who went in could ever find the way out. In the middle of the maze lived the Minotaur, a monster that was half man and half bull.

Every year, King Minos made the city of Athens send fourteen young people to Crete, to be sent into the Labyrinth. None of them ever came back.

One year, Prince Theseus of Athens stepped forward. “I will go,” he said, “and I will stop the Minotaur for ever.”

When he arrived in Crete, the king’s daughter, Ariadne, secretly came to him. She pressed a ball of golden thread into his hand. “Tie one end by the door,” she whispered, “and unwind it as you go.”

Theseus crept into the darkness, unwinding the thread behind him. At the centre of the maze, the Minotaur charged, bellowing. Theseus was quick and strong, and after a long struggle the monster lay still.

Then Theseus followed the golden thread, turn by turn, all the way back to the light.

Icarus and the Wings

Daedalus was the cleverest inventor in all of Greece. But King Minos of Crete had locked him in a tall tower with his son, Icarus, so that he could never leave the island.

“Minos rules the land and the sea,” said Daedalus, “but he does not rule the sky.”

For many weeks he collected feathers dropped by the birds. He laid them in rows, the long ones and the short ones, and fixed them together with thread and wax. At last he had made two pairs of wings.

He fastened the wings to his son’s arms. “Listen carefully,” he said. “Do not fly too low, or the sea spray will make your feathers heavy. Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax. Follow me.”

They leapt from the tower and soared out over the sea. Icarus whooped with joy. It was wonderful! He forgot his father’s warning and climbed higher and higher, up towards the blazing sun.

The wax grew soft. One by one, the feathers slipped away. Icarus flapped his bare arms, but it was no use. He tumbled down into the sea far below, and Daedalus flew on alone, weeping.

Icarus and the Wings

Daedalus was the cleverest inventor in all of Greece. But King Minos of Crete had locked him in a tall tower with his son, Icarus, so that he could never leave the island.

“Minos rules the land and the sea,” said Daedalus, “but he does not rule the sky.”

For many weeks he collected feathers dropped by the birds. He laid them in rows, the long ones and the short ones, and fixed them together with thread and wax. At last he had made two pairs of wings.

He fastened the wings to his son’s arms. “Listen carefully,” he said. “Do not fly too low, or the sea spray will make your feathers heavy. Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax. Follow me.”

They leapt from the tower and soared out over the sea. Icarus whooped with joy. It was wonderful! He forgot his father’s warning and climbed higher and higher, up towards the blazing sun.

The wax grew soft. One by one, the feathers slipped away. Icarus flapped his bare arms, but it was no use. He tumbled down into the sea far below, and Daedalus flew on alone, weeping.

The Sword in the Stone

When the old king of Britain died, he left no son to rule after him. The lords quarrelled and fought, and the land fell into trouble.

Then, one winter morning, a strange thing appeared in a churchyard in London: a great stone, and stuck deep in the stone was a shining sword. Golden letters were written on it: “Whoever pulls this sword out of this stone is the true king of Britain.”

One by one, the strongest knights in the land took hold of the sword. They heaved and they strained until their faces turned red, but the sword did not move at all.

On New Year’s Day there was a great tournament. A boy called Arthur had come to London to help his older brother, Sir Kay. But Kay had left his sword at home! Arthur ran to fetch it, but the house was locked.

Hurrying back, Arthur passed the churchyard and saw the sword in the stone. “That will do for Kay,” he thought. He took hold of the handle and pulled. The sword slid out as easily as a spoon from a pot of honey.

When the lords saw what Arthur had done, they knelt before him. The wizard Merlin smiled. He had known all along who the true king would be.

St George and the Dragon

Outside a town called Silene, there was a lake, and in the lake lived a dragon. Its breath was poisonous, and its roar shook the walls of the town. To keep the dragon away, the frightened people fed it two sheep every day.

Soon there were no sheep left. The king was in despair, because now the dragon wanted a person instead. Lots were drawn, and the name that came out was the king’s own daughter, the princess.

The princess walked bravely down to the lake. Just then, a knight came riding by on a white horse. His name was George.

“Why are you crying?” asked George. “Run away, good knight,” said the princess, “or the dragon will eat you too!”

But George did not run. When the dragon rose out of the water, he made the sign of the cross, lowered his lance and charged. The lance struck the dragon and it crashed to the ground.

The people of the town cheered and cheered. Today St George is the patron saint of England, and his day is celebrated on 23 April.

Storm at the Speedway

The sky over the Speedway was the colour of a bruise. Turbo sat on the grid, his engine ticking, while the crowd huddled under umbrellas.

“It’s going to pour,” said Rosa over the radio. “We’ve put on the tyres with the deepest grooves. You’ll be slower at first, but trust them.”

The lights went out. Blaze shot ahead on his smooth dry-weather tyres, and Turbo slipped back to fifth. Two laps later, the clouds burst. Rain hammered on the track like a thousand drums.

Blaze’s tyres could not grip. At the hairpin bend he slid wide, spinning gently round until he faced the wrong way. Turbo slowed, steered carefully round him and called on the radio, “Blaze has spun at the hairpin! Tell the marshals!”

One by one, the cars on dry tyres skated off the track. Turbo’s grooved tyres pushed the water away, and he crept up to second place, then first.

After the race, a soggy Blaze rolled up beside him. “You could have just driven past me,” he said. “Why did you warn the marshals?”

Turbo flashed his headlights. “Because winning only counts,” he said, “if everyone gets home safely.”

Storm at the Speedway

The sky over the Speedway was the colour of a bruise. Turbo sat on the grid, his engine ticking, while the crowd huddled under umbrellas.

“It’s going to pour,” said Rosa over the radio. “We’ve put on the tyres with the deepest grooves. You’ll be slower at first, but trust them.”

The lights went out. Blaze shot ahead on his smooth dry-weather tyres, and Turbo slipped back to fifth. Two laps later, the clouds burst. Rain hammered on the track like a thousand drums.

Blaze’s tyres could not grip. At the hairpin bend he slid wide, spinning gently round until he faced the wrong way. Turbo slowed, steered carefully round him and called on the radio, “Blaze has spun at the hairpin! Tell the marshals!”

One by one, the cars on dry tyres skated off the track. Turbo’s grooved tyres pushed the water away, and he crept up to second place, then first.

After the race, a soggy Blaze rolled up beside him. “You could have just driven past me,” he said. “Why did you warn the marshals?”

Turbo flashed his headlights. “Because winning only counts,” he said, “if everyone gets home safely.”

Captain Nova and the Meteor Storm

The alarm screeched across the bridge of the starship Comet. Bleep the robot spun round in circles, his lights flashing red.

“Meteor storm!” he beeped. “Thousands of rocks, coming straight for us!”

Captain Nova studied the screen. The meteors were spread out like a swarm of angry bees, far too wide to fly around. Her ship’s shield was weak; a single big rock could crack it.

Then she noticed something. Beside them floated a tiny grey moon, no bigger than a city.

“Bleep,” she said calmly, “if we hide behind that moon, what will the meteors hit?”

Bleep’s lights flickered while he thought. “The moon!” he cried. “The moon will be our shield!”

Captain Nova steered the Comet into the moon’s shadow. Moments later, the storm arrived. Rocks pounded the far side of the little moon, sending up silent clouds of dust, but not one of them touched the ship.

When the last meteor had whizzed past, Bleep did a happy spin. “How did you stay so calm?”

Captain Nova smiled. “Panicking uses up your brain,” she said. “Staying calm leaves room to think.”

{hero} and the Great Flood

For three days and nights the rain did not stop. On the fourth morning, the river burst its banks and brown water began to swirl through the streets of Millbrook.

{hero} landed in the town square with a whoosh. “Everyone stay calm!” the hero called. “I’ll stop this flood!”

But there was too much water, even for a superhero. Each time {hero} pushed one wave back, two more rushed in somewhere else.

Then an old man in a flat cap tapped the hero on the shoulder. “Begging your pardon,” he said, “but we’ve got thousands of sandbags at the builder’s yard. We just can’t carry them fast enough.”

{hero} grinned. “Then let’s do it together!”

The people of Millbrook formed a long line, passing sandbags from hand to hand. {hero} flew the heaviest piles to the very front. Children carried small bags. Grandparents tied the knots. Slowly, a wall of sandbags grew along the river, higher and higher, until the water could not get over.

That evening, the whole town stood muddy and soaking wet, but smiling. “I’ve learned something today,” said {hero}. “Even a superhero is stronger with a team.”

items.passage:
Fact file: The Roman army

The Roman army was one of the best-trained armies in the ancient world. In AD 43, the Emperor Claudius sent it to invade Britain.

The army was split into legions. Each legion had about 5,000 soldiers, called legionaries. Legionaries were split into groups of about 80 men, each led by an officer called a centurion.

A legionary carried a large curved shield, called a scutum, a short sword, a dagger and two throwing spears. He wore a metal helmet and armour made of metal strips.

Roman soldiers could march about 20 miles in a day, carrying all their equipment on their backs. At the end of each day’s march, they built a camp with a ditch and a wall around it.

In battle, soldiers sometimes formed a “testudo”, which means tortoise. They held their shields above their heads and around their sides, so that arrows bounced off, like rain off a tortoise’s shell.

Glossary
legion: a large group of Roman soldiers

Fact file: The Roman army

The Roman army was one of the best-trained armies in the ancient world. In AD 43, the Emperor Claudius sent it to invade Britain.

The army was split into legions. Each legion had about 5,000 soldiers, called legionaries. Legionaries were split into groups of about 80 men, each led by an officer called a centurion.

A legionary carried a large curved shield, called a scutum, a short sword, a dagger and two throwing spears. He wore a metal helmet and armour made of metal strips.

Roman soldiers could march about 20 miles in a day, carrying all their equipment on their backs. At the end of each day’s march, they built a camp with a ditch and a wall around it.

In battle, soldiers sometimes formed a “testudo”, which means tortoise. They held their shields above their heads and around their sides, so that arrows bounced off, like rain off a tortoise’s shell.

centurion: an officer in charge of about 80 men

Fact file: The planets

Our Earth is one of eight planets that travel around the Sun. The time it takes a planet to go once around the Sun is called its year.

The four planets closest to the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. Mercury is the closest to the Sun and the smallest planet. Venus is the hottest, because its thick blanket of air traps the heat. Mars looks red because its dust contains rust.

The four outer planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, are giants made mostly of gas and ice. Jupiter is the biggest planet of all: more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it! Saturn has beautiful rings made of chunks of ice and rock. Neptune is the furthest from the Sun, so it is dark and freezing cold.

Earth is the only planet where we know there is life. It is just the right distance from the Sun: not too hot and not too cold, so there is liquid water.

items.passage:
Fact file: Honeybees

Honeybees live together in a nest called a hive. A busy hive can hold more than 50,000 bees!

Every hive has three kinds of bee. There is one queen, who lays all the eggs. There are thousands of workers, which are all female. And there are some drones, which are male.

The workers do almost all the jobs. They clean the hive, look after the young bees, guard the entrance and fly out to collect nectar and pollen from flowers. They turn the sweet nectar into honey, which they store to eat in the winter.

When a worker bee finds lots of flowers, she flies back to the hive and does a special dance, called the waggle dance. The dance tells the other bees which way to fly and how far to go.

As bees fly from flower to flower, they carry pollen with them. This helps the plants make seeds and fruit. Without bees, there would be far fewer apples, strawberries and tomatoes.

items.passage:
Three of us afloat in the meadow by the swing,
Three of us abroad in the basket on the lea.
Winds are in the air, they are blowing in the spring,
And waves are on the meadow like the waves there are at sea.

Where shall we adventure, to-day that we’re afloat,
Wary of the weather and steering by a star?
Shall it be to Africa, a-steering of the boat,
To Providence, or Babylon or off to Malabar?

Hi!  but here’s a squadron a-rowing on the sea—
Cattle on the meadow a-charging with a roar!
Quick, and we’ll escape them, they’re as mad as they can be,
The wicket is the harbour and the garden is the shore.

items.passage:
When I was sick and lay a-bed,
I had two pillows at my head,
And all my toys beside me lay,
To keep me happy all the day.

And sometimes for an hour or so
I watched my leaden soldiers go,
With different uniforms and drills,
Among the bed-clothes, through the hills;

And sometimes sent my ships in fleets
All up and down among the sheets;
Or brought my trees and houses out,
And planted cities all about.

I was the giant great and still
That sits upon the pillow-hill,

While I was young I lived upon my mother’s milk, as I could not eat grass. In the daytime I ran by her side, and at night I lay down close by her. When it was hot we used to stand by the pond in the shade of the trees, and when it was cold we had a nice warm shed near the grove.

As soon as I was old enough to eat grass my mother used to go out to work in the daytime, and come back in the evening.

There were six young colts in the meadow besides me; they were older than I was; some were nearly as large as grown-up horses. I used to run with them, and had great fun; we used to gallop all together round and round the field as hard as we could go. Sometimes we had rather rough play, for they would frequently bite and kick as well as gallop.

One day, when there was a good deal of kicking, my mother whinnied to me to come to her, and then she said:

“I wish you to pay attention to what I am going to say to you. The colts who live here are very good colts, but they are cart-horse colts, and of course they have not learned manners. You have been well-bred and well-born; your father has a great name in these parts, and your grandfather won the cup two years at the Newmarket races; your grandmother had the sweetest temper of any horse I ever knew, and I think you have never seen me kick or bite. I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn bad ways; do your work with a good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never bite or kick even in play.”
items.passageSource: Anna Sewell, Black Beauty (1877), chapter 1
